cards.q: Define the internal energy of a body.
cards.a: The sum of the randomly distributed kinetic energies and potential energies of all its particles.

cards.q: State two ways of increasing the internal energy of a system.
cards.a: By heating it (transferring energy to it because of a temperature difference), or by doing work on it, for example compressing a gas.

cards.q: While a substance is changing state, what happens to the kinetic and the potential energies of its particles?
cards.a: The potential energies change, as the particles move further apart or closer together. The kinetic energies do not change, so the temperature stays constant.

cards.q: Define specific heat capacity.
cards.a: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K, without a change of state. Unit: \(\text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\).

cards.q: Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 0.50 kg of water by 20 K. (specific heat capacity of water \(4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(4.2 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}\)

cards.q: A 50 W heater runs for 120 s and raises the temperature of a 0.25 kg metal block by 12 K. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal, assuming no energy is lost.
cards.a: \(2.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\)

cards.q: In an electrical method for specific heat capacity, energy is lost to the surroundings. How does this affect the value obtained, and how is it reduced?
cards.a: The value comes out too high: more energy is supplied than actually heats the substance. It is reduced by insulating the block or container.

cards.q: Define specific latent heat.
cards.a: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature. Unit: \(\text{J kg}^{-1}\).
cards.why: Fusion is for melting or freezing; vaporisation is for boiling or condensing.

cards.q: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.20 kg of ice at 0 °C. (specific latent heat of fusion of ice \(3.3 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(6.6 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}\)

cards.q: Calculate the energy needed to turn 0.10 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 20 °C. (latent heat of fusion \(3.3 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\); specific heat capacity of water \(4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(4.1 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}\)
cards.why: Treat each stage separately: a change of state, then a change of temperature.

cards.q: Water flows through a heater at \(0.040\ \text{kg s}^{-1}\) and its temperature rises by 15 K. Calculate the power transferred to the water. (specific heat capacity \(4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(2.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{W}\)
steps: Each second, 0.040 kg of water is heated by 15 K.
cards.why: In continuous flow, the mass per second takes the place of the mass, and the answer is a power.

cards.q: A solid is heated at a constant rate until it has boiled. What do the flat sections of its temperature–time graph show?
cards.a: Changes of state: melting, then boiling. The energy supplied is increasing the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy, so the temperature does not rise.

cards.q: Outline an experiment to determine the specific latent heat of fusion of ice.
cards.a: Melt ice with an electrical heater and measure the mass melted by a known amount of energy.
marks: Put crushed ice at 0 °C in two funnels over beakers. Place an immersion heater in one; the other is a control.
Switch the heater on for a measured time, recording the potential difference and the current to find the energy supplied, \(E = VIt\).
Measure the mass of water collected from each funnel.
Subtract the control's mass, to allow for ice melted by the room, giving the mass melted by the heater.
\(L = \frac{E}{\Delta m}\).

cards.q: Outline how to calibrate a thermistor in a potential divider so that it can be used as a thermostat.
cards.a: Record the divider's output at known temperatures and use the calibration graph to set the switching point.
marks: Connect the thermistor in series with a fixed resistor across a supply, and measure the potential difference across one of them.
Place the thermistor in a water bath with a thermometer.
Record the output potential difference over a range of temperatures as the water is heated or cools.
Plot the output potential difference against temperature: this is the calibration curve.
Read from the curve the potential difference at the required temperature, and set the circuit to switch at that value.

cards.q: What is absolute zero?
cards.a: The lowest possible temperature, 0 K (−273 °C), at which the particles of a substance have their minimum kinetic energy.

cards.q: A gas is heated from 20 °C to 40 °C at constant volume. A student says its pressure doubles. Why is this wrong?
cards.a: Gas equations use the absolute temperature in kelvin. The temperature rises from 293 K to 313 K, an increase of only about 7%, so the pressure rises by about 7%.
cards.why: Add 273 to a Celsius temperature before using it in any gas equation.

cards.q: State Boyle's law.
cards.a: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure is inversely proportional to the volume: \(pV = \text{constant}\).

cards.q: State Charles's law.
cards.a: For a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, the volume is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.

cards.q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, how is the pressure related to the temperature?
cards.a: The pressure is directly proportional to the absolute temperature (the pressure law).

cards.q: Write the ideal gas equation for \(N\) molecules, and say what each symbol means.
cards.a: \(pV = NkT\): \(p\) pressure, \(V\) volume, \(N\) number of molecules, \(k\) the Boltzmann constant, \(T\) absolute temperature.

cards.q: Write the ideal gas equation for \(n\) moles of gas, and state how the molar gas constant \(R\) is related to the Boltzmann constant \(k\).
cards.a: \(pV = nRT\), and \(k = \frac{R}{N_{A}}\), where \(N_{A}\) is the Avogadro constant.

cards.q: A gas has a pressure of \(1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}\), a volume of \(1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}\) and a temperature of 300 K. Calculate the number of molecules. (\(k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(2.4 \times 10^{22}\)

cards.q: A gas at 20 °C has a pressure of \(1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}\) and a volume of \(2.4 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^{3}\). Calculate the number of moles. (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: 0.99 mol

cards.q: What is meant by the molar mass of a substance?
cards.a: The mass of one mole of the substance: the mass of \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\) of its particles.
cards.why: Molecular mass is the mass of one molecule: molar mass ÷ the Avogadro constant.

cards.q: A gas expands by \(2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}\) at a constant pressure of \(1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}\). Calculate the work done by the gas.
cards.a: 200 J

cards.q: Outline how to investigate the relationship between the pressure and the volume of a gas at constant temperature.
cards.a: Change the volume of a trapped gas in steps and record the pressure each time.
marks: Trap a fixed mass of gas in a sealed syringe or tube, connected to a pressure gauge.
Change the volume in steps and record the volume and the pressure at each.
Wait after each change before reading, so the gas returns to room temperature.
Plot \(p\) against \(\frac{1}{V}\): a straight line through the origin shows \(p \propto \frac{1}{V}\).

cards.q: Outline how to investigate Charles's law, and how the results give a value for absolute zero.
cards.a: Heat a trapped column of gas at constant pressure and measure its length at each temperature.
marks: Trap a column of air in a capillary tube, sealed at the bottom, with a small bead of liquid above it; the top is open, so the pressure stays constant.
Put the tube in a water bath with a thermometer, alongside a ruler.
Record the length of the air column (proportional to its volume) over a range of temperatures.
Plot length against temperature in °C: a straight line.
Extend the line back to zero length: it meets the temperature axis at absolute zero.

cards.q: What is Brownian motion, and what is it evidence for?
cards.a: The random, jerky motion of small visible particles, such as smoke particles in air. It is evidence that the air is made of much smaller, fast-moving molecules that collide with them.

cards.q: State the assumptions of the kinetic theory model of an ideal gas.
cards.a: The molecules are tiny, move randomly, and interact only in elastic collisions.
marks: The gas contains a very large number of molecules in rapid, random motion.
The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.
All collisions, between molecules and with the walls, are perfectly elastic.
There are no forces between molecules except during collisions.
The time of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions.

cards.q: Explain how the molecules of a gas exert a pressure on the walls of their container.
cards.a: Molecules hitting the walls change momentum, which needs a force.
marks: Molecules collide with the walls and rebound, so their momentum changes.
By Newton's second law, the wall exerts a force on each molecule equal to its rate of change of momentum.
By Newton's third law, each molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall.
Pressure is the total force of all these collisions divided by the area of the wall.

cards.q: Outline the derivation of \(pV = \frac{1}{3}Nm(c_{\text{rms}})^{2}\) for an ideal gas in a cubic box of side \(L\).
cards.a: \(pV = \frac{1}{3}Nm(c_{\text{rms}})^{2}\)
steps: One molecule of mass \(m\) moving at \(u\) hits a wall and rebounds: its change of momentum is \(2mu\).
It returns to that wall after a time \(\frac{2L}{u}\), so the average force it exerts is \(\frac{2mu}{2L/u} = \frac{mu^{2}}{L}\) (Newton's second and third laws).
Pressure from this molecule: force ÷ area \(= \frac{mu^{2}}{L^{3}} = \frac{mu^{2}}{V}\).
Motion is random in three dimensions, so \(\overline{u^{2}} = \frac{1}{3}(c_{\text{rms}})^{2}\), giving \(pV = \frac{1}{3}Nm(c_{\text{rms}})^{2}\).

cards.q: Use the kinetic theory to explain why the pressure of a gas rises when it is heated at constant volume.
cards.a: Faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often.
marks: A higher temperature means a greater average kinetic energy, so the molecules move faster.
Each collision with a wall gives a larger change of momentum.
The molecules also hit the walls more often.
So the rate of change of momentum, and therefore the force on the walls, is greater: the pressure rises.

cards.q: Use the kinetic theory to explain why halving the volume of a gas at constant temperature doubles its pressure.
cards.a: The molecules hit the walls twice as often.
marks: The temperature is constant, so the molecules' average speed does not change.
In half the volume the molecules are twice as closely packed.
They collide with each unit area of wall twice as often.
The change of momentum per collision is the same, so the pressure doubles.

cards.q: What is the root mean square speed of the molecules of a gas?
cards.a: The square root of the mean of the squares of the speeds of the molecules.
cards.why: It is used because the kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so it is the mean of the squares that matters.

cards.q: Write the equation linking the mean kinetic energy of a gas molecule to the absolute temperature.
cards.why: The mean kinetic energy depends only on the temperature: at the same temperature, molecules of every gas have the same mean kinetic energy.

cards.q: Derive \(\frac{1}{2}m(c_{\text{rms}})^{2} = \frac{3}{2}kT\) from the kinetic theory equation and the ideal gas equation.
Calculate the mean kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 300 K. (\(k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(6.2 \times 10^{-21}\ \text{J}\)

cards.q: Calculate the root mean square speed of nitrogen molecules at 300 K. (mass of a nitrogen molecule \(4.65 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg}\); \(k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(520\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Leaving out the final square root is a common slip.

cards.q: A student says the internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. What is wrong for an ideal gas?
cards.a: An ideal gas has no forces between its molecules, so they have no potential energy. Its internal energy is the total kinetic energy of the molecules only.

cards.q: What is the difference in origin between the gas laws and the kinetic theory equation?
cards.a: The gas laws are empirical: they come from experimental measurements. The kinetic theory equation is theoretical: it is derived from assumptions about how molecules behave.
